pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second and only stressed syllable, SIST, which rhymes with 'list'. Do not add a vowel between s and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and works in all contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'consist of' in writing and formal speech to describe what something is made of, as in 'The team consists of five people.' In casual speech they often say 'is made up of' or 'includes' instead. It is never followed directly by a noun without 'of', except in the sense 'consist in' (to lie in).

distinctions.note: Consist of lists the complete makeup of something; include suggests the items are only part of a larger whole.
Comprise means to contain or be made of; in careful American writing, prefer 'comprises' for the whole and avoid 'is comprised of'.

examples.everyday: My lunch usually consists of a sandwich and an apple.
examples.professional: The dataset consists of roughly two million records, split into training and test sets.
examples.analytical: Aristotle held that a good life consists in the activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a sandwich, which is nothing more than its bread, filling, and sauce put together.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consistere, 'to stand together', from com- 'together' and sistere 'to stand'.
common_mistakes: Using 'consist' without 'of' in the sense of being made up of, as in 'The team consists five people'.
Using the continuous form, as in 'is consisting of'; it is a stative verb and is not used that way.

consist.etymology: From Middle French *consister*, from Latin *consistō* (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from *com-* (“together”) + *sistō* (“to cause to stand, stand”).

senses.definition: A disease spread by contact.
The spread or transmission of such a disease.
The spread of anything likened to a contagious disease.
senses.example: Panic spread like contagion through the crowd after one person shouted about a fire.

senses.definition: The passing on of manners or behavior through a closed community or household.
senses.example: Living in that isolated household, the children absorbed their uncle's rough manners through pure contagion.

senses.definition: The spread of (initially small) shocks, which initially affect only a few financial institutions or a particular region of an economy, to other financial sectors and other countries whose economies were previously healthy.
senses.example: Economists warned that the contagion from one bank's collapse could spread to healthy economies overseas.

senses.definition: A recession or crisis developed in such manner.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: A disease that spreads from person to person, or the spread of a harmful idea or behavior through a group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the -TAY- syllable. The -gion ending sounds like juhn, with the g pronounced as a j, so do not say con-TAY-gee-on.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests danger and something that spreads out of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contagion mostly in news, public health and literary writing, as in 'the contagion spread through the city.' In everyday speech people say 'the bug,' 'it's going around' or 'it's contagious.' Figuratively, contagion describes panic, rumors or trends that spread quickly, usually with a negative tone.

distinctions.note: An infection is an invasion of germs in one person; contagion stresses that the disease can spread from person to person.
An epidemic is a sudden rise in cases in one area; contagion describes the transmissible quality of the disease or idea.
A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic; contagion does not specify the scale.

examples.everyday: Stay home if you're sick so you don't spread the contagion to the office.
examples.professional: Our safety plan limits contagion by spacing out desks and asking sick staff to work from home.
examples.analytical: Sociologists often describe panic as a social contagion, in which fear spreads from person to person without any physical agent.

nuance.analogy: Contagion is like a wildfire: one spark can spread through dry grass until the whole field burns.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contagio, contact or touch, from contingere, to touch upon.
common_mistakes: Using contagion for a single sick person; it refers to the spread or the transmitted disease.
Confusing the noun contagion with the adjective contagious; say 'contagious' to describe something that spreads.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the -TAY- syllable.

contagion.etymology: From Middle English (late 14th century), from Old French, from Latin *contāgiō* (“a touching, contact, contagion”) related to *contingō* (“touch closely”).

senses.definition: The action of continuing.
The period during which something continues or goes on; duration.
senses.example: The continuance of the drought threatened the farmers' harvest through the entire summer.

senses.definition: An order issued by a court granting a postponement of a legal proceeding for a set period.
senses.example: The judge granted a continuance, pushing the trial date back until the following spring.

core.definition: The fact or process of continuing; the length of time something keeps going, or the act of carrying it on.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TIN, and the last syllable is a light uns. The -yoo- is a single quick sound, so say kuhn-TIN-yoo-uns, not KON-tin-yoo-ants.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds formal and is often used in legal or business writing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday speech Americans say keep going or continuation; continuance sounds stiff outside formal or legal settings. In US courts, a continuance is a postponement of a hearing or trial, so a lawyer may file a motion for a continuance. In business writing it can refer to the ongoing life of an agreement or company.

distinctions.note: Continuance stresses the fact or length of going on and is often formal or legal; continuation is more common and can mean the next part of something.
Continuity is the quality of being unbroken or consistent over time; continuance is simply the fact of going on or how long it lasts.

examples.everyday: We are hoping for the continuance of this nice weather through the weekend.
examples.professional: Legal wants a continuance on the contract signing, so we need to push the deadline to Friday.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that personal identity depends on the continuance of memory and character through time.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that keeps flowing; its continuance depends on a steady supply of water.
nuance.etymology: From continue plus -ance, from Latin continuare, 'to join together', from continuus, 'uninterrupted'.
common_mistakes: Using continuance in casual talk where continuation or keep going sounds more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying KON-tin-yoo-ants, instead of kuhn-TIN-yoo-uns.

continuance.etymology: From Middle English *continuance*, *contynuaunce*, from Old French *continuance*, from *continuer*.

senses.definition: An approach where teams produce software in short cycles, ensuring that the software can be reliably released at any time.

core.definition: An approach where teams build software in short cycles so it can be released reliably at any time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIV in delivery and keep a lighter stress on TIN in continuous. The final 'ery' is a reduced 'uh-ree', not 'air-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in software and business settings, where it signals speed and reliability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly among software engineers, DevOps teams and tech managers, in meetings, job postings and documentation. It is not used in everyday conversation. Do not confuse it with continuous deployment, which goes further by releasing every approved change to users automatically.

distinctions.note: Continuous delivery keeps software ready to release, often with a manual approval step; continuous deployment automatically releases every change.
Continuous integration merges and tests code changes frequently; continuous delivery extends this to keeping the software releasable.

examples.everyday: My friend asked about my job, so I said our team uses continuous delivery, which means we can ship updates almost every day.
examples.professional: We're moving the payments service to continuous delivery so every merged change goes to staging automatically.
examples.analytical: Continuous delivery treats release readiness as a property of the codebase rather than a special event at the end of a project.

nuance.analogy: Like a bakery that keeps the oven hot so fresh bread is always ready, instead of baking one big batch each quarter.
nuance.etymology: Compound of continuous and delivery; the term was popularized by Jez Humble and David Farley's 2010 book Continuous Delivery.
common_mistakes: Using continuous delivery to mean continuous deployment, which is a different practice.
Stressing 'continuous' too heavily and losing the stress on 'DE-liv-ery' in the phrase.

senses.definition: A person or thing that converts.
senses.example: The pastor was a famous converter who won hundreds of new members to the faith.

senses.definition: A device that changes voltage or frequency, for example one that converts alternating current to direct current.
senses.example: The laptop charger is actually a converter that changes wall power to direct current.

senses.definition: A retort or furnace, used e.g. in the Bessemer process, in which molten cast iron is decarburized and converted into steel by a blast of air forced through the liquid metal.
senses.example: The steelworks poured molten iron into the converter, forcing air through the metal to make steel.

senses.definition: A reaction chamber in which exhaust gases are catalytically converted to carbon dioxide.
senses.example: The car's catalytic converter reduces carbon monoxide before exhaust leaves the tailpipe.

senses.definition: A program that converts one file format to another one, or which converts between different units of measurement, such as miles to meters.
senses.example: I used a file converter to change the old documents into PDF format.

senses.definition: A device that converts an analogue to a digital signal, or vice versa.
senses.example: The sound card's analog-to-digital converter samples the microphone input thousands of times per second.

senses.definition: Regional term for remote control.
senses.example: Grandma couldn't find the converter, so she called for help to change the channel.

senses.definition: A patient with a certain condition that subsequently develops into another condition.
senses.example: Doctors tracked the converter, a patient whose benign lesion later became a malignant tumor.

core.definition: A device or person that changes something into another form, such as a device that changes electrical current or voltage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. Between the vowels, the t is usually flapped, so it sounds like a quick 'd,' and the final -er is an unstressed r-colored schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes a tool or process, so it has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, the most common use is 'catalytic converter,' the car part that cleans exhaust. Americans also use 'currency converter' when traveling or shopping online. In engineering and electronics, the word is used for devices that change voltage or signal format. Telling someone 'you're a converter' would sound strange unless you mean a person who changes others' beliefs.

distinctions.note: An adapter changes the shape of a plug or connection without changing the electrical current or voltage; a converter changes the electrical properties themselves.
A transformer changes voltage using electromagnetic induction, and it works only with alternating current; a converter can change alternating to direct current as well.

examples.everyday: My mechanic said I need a new catalytic converter, and it's going to be expensive.
examples.professional: The analog-to-digital converter is sampling the sensor at one kilohertz, which is too slow for this application.
examples.analytical: In Kant's system, the schematism works as a converter between pure concepts and empirical intuitions.

nuance.analogy: Like a currency exchange booth: it takes one form of money and gives you another.
nuance.etymology: From convert (verb) plus the suffix -er, 'one who or that which does something.'
common_mistakes: Confusing converter with adapter when the device must change voltage, not just the plug shape.
Pronouncing the middle t as a hard t instead of a flap.

senses.definition: To make someone believe, or feel sure about something, especially by using logic, argument or evidence.
senses.example: I wouldn't have or do something, unless I'm convinced that it's good.

senses.definition: To persuade.
senses.example: I finally convinced my brother to try the new ramen place downtown.

senses.definition: To behave believably in a role; to make someone perceive oneself as the character being portrayed.
senses.example: The young actor convinced audiences that he had spent years at sea.

core.definition: To cause someone to believe, or feel sure, that something is true, usually through argument, reasons or evidence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and keep the first vowel reduced to a schwa. The -nce ending is pronounced like 'ns', so the word is one short syllable with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes changing someone's mind by legitimate means; it can sound pushy if you keep trying after someone has said no.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use convince all the time in everyday talk, usually with a person as the object: 'convince someone to,' 'convince someone that,' or 'convince someone of something.' The sense 'to behave believably in a role' is theatrical and less common in ordinary conversation. A natural reply when someone resists is 'Come on, let me convince you' or 'You don't have to convince me.'

distinctions.note: Persuade focuses on getting someone to act or decide, while convince focuses on getting someone to believe something.
Convince is the verb that causes the belief, while convinced is the adjective describing the person who now believes.

examples.everyday: I finally convinced my roommate to try the new taco place on Fourth Street.
examples.professional: We need solid load-test numbers to convince the product team that the migration is safe.
examples.analytical: Descartes sought an argument that could convince the skeptic that the self's existence is certain.

nuance.analogy: Convincing someone is like building a bridge of reasons from their doubt to your conclusion, one plank at a time.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convincere, to overcome, refute or prove.
common_mistakes: Saying convince to someone or convince someone to do, forgetting the object: correct is convince someone to do something.
Using persuade and convince interchangeably; persuade is about action, convince is about belief.

convince.etymology: Latin *convincō* (“to refute, prove”), from *con-* + *vincō* (“to conquer, vanquish”).

senses.definition: A wide, flat metal pan suitable for baking in an oven.

core.definition: A flat metal pan, usually with no sides or only a low rim, used for baking cookies and other foods in an oven.

pronunciation.tip: Americans stress COOKIE, not SHEET, because this is a compound noun. The first syllable of cookie has the short oo of book, and sheet has a long ee, not the vowel of shit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical kitchen word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase constantly in home baking, and it is what most people call the pan. Asking a store clerk 'Where are the cookie sheets?' is completely natural. People also say 'baking sheet' or 'sheet pan,' and in everyday speech the three terms are often interchangeable.

distinctions.note: Nearly the same item. 'Baking sheet' is the more general term, while 'cookie sheet' is the everyday home word.
A baking pan has high sides for cakes or casseroles, while a cookie sheet is flat with little or no rim.

collocations: line a cookie sheet with parchment paper

examples.everyday: Can you grab a cookie sheet from the bottom drawer? The dough is ready to go in.
examples.professional: Please count the cookie sheets in the test kitchen before we move the recipe to the commercial oven.
examples.analytical: A thin aluminum cookie sheet heats quickly and unevenly, which is why bakers often stack two sheets to protect the bottoms of the cookies.

nuance.analogy: A cookie sheet is like a flat stage for the oven: it holds the dough while the heat does the work.
nuance.etymology: Cookie comes from Dutch koekje, 'little cake'; sheet comes from an Old English word for a broad piece of material.
common_mistakes: Saying 'cookie tray' or 'cookie plate' for this flat pan; Americans say 'sheet.'
Putting the main stress on the second word (cookie SHEET) instead of COOKie sheet.
Thinking 'sheet' means only paper; a cookie sheet is a metal pan.

senses.definition: Anything which cools.
senses.example: The new fan is a much better cooler than the old window unit.

senses.definition: An insulated bin or box used with ice or freezer packs to keep food or beverages cold while picnicking or camping.
A device for refrigerating dead bodies in a morgue.
senses.example: The morgue's cooler was full, so the hospital sent two bodies to the county facility.

senses.definition: Samalamig drink (sweet chilled beverage, such as chilled fruit juice or other flavors like chocolate, coffee, sweet corn, etc. usually mixed with either shredded jelly and/or sago pearls or tapioca pearls)
senses.example: My aunt bought a plastic cup of cooler with sago pearls from the Filipino vendor.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of air cooler, evaporative cooler, desert cooler, or swamp cooler.
A prison.
senses.example: They locked him up in the cooler for three months after the bar fight.

senses.definition: A bouncer or doorman.
senses.example: The cooler at the back door wouldn't let anyone in without an ID.

senses.definition: A cold deck.
A loss suffered while holding a hand which is ordinarily strong, especially one which involves the loss of many chips.
senses.example: He lost a huge pot on a cooler, holding two kings against a full house.

core.definition: An insulated box filled with ice to keep food and drinks cold, especially for picnics, camping or beach trips.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'er' is a reduced, rhotic sound, so say it as 'ler' with the r pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, a cooler is the standard word for the portable insulated box people take on picnics, camping trips or beach days. It is often called an ice chest in some regions, especially in the South and Midwest. If you say 'ice box,' some older Americans may think of an old-fashioned refrigerator.

distinctions.note: Ice chest is a regional synonym, common in parts of the South and Midwest; cooler is the more widely understood term.
A refrigerator is a fixed appliance powered by electricity; a cooler is portable and uses ice or freezer packs.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the cooler from the trunk? The drinks are in it.
examples.professional: We'll need two coolers for the field trip, so please put the lunches on the ice before we leave.
examples.analytical: The cooler, as a device, reveals how modern leisure depends on the temporary control of temperature.

nuance.analogy: A cooler is a small, portable refrigerator with no plug, relying on ice to keep things cold.
nuance.etymology: Formed from cool and the suffix -er, meaning a thing that cools.
common_mistakes: Using cooler to mean a cool temperature; the adjective is cool, while cooler is the comparative or the noun for a box.
Saying 'cooler' for a refrigerator in a house; in American homes, refrigerator or fridge is the normal word.

conversation.text: Can you grab a soda for me from the cooler?
We packed a cooler with sandwiches, fruit, and drinks.
It's a little cooler by the water, so let's sit over there.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to correction; serving to correct.
senses.example: As the currents were changing rapidly, the captain had to make many corrective course changes.

senses.definition: Something that corrects or counteracts something.
senses.example: alkalies are correctives of acids

core.definition: Intended to fix, improve, or counteract something that is wrong or harmful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REK. The -ive ending reduces to 'iv', not 'eeve'. Don't stress the first syllable, as in KOR-ek-tiv.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it implies improvement rather than punishment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use corrective in medicine (corrective lenses, corrective surgery), education, and the workplace (corrective action, corrective feedback). In everyday speech they say fix or make it right. Corrective is more formal and often describes measures or actions rather than people.

distinctions.note: Remedial means designed to remedy a deficiency, often in education; corrective is broader and more about fixing a particular error or condition.
Punitive means meant to punish; corrective is meant to fix or improve, not penalize.

examples.everyday: My eye doctor said I need corrective lenses for reading, not just glasses for distance.
examples.professional: We've taken corrective action on the server issue, so the outage shouldn't happen again.
examples.analytical: In Aristotle's account, corrective justice restores the balance disturbed by an unjust transaction.

nuance.analogy: Corrective is like a pair of glasses: they don't change the world, they adjust what you see so it becomes clear.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin correctivus, from Latin corrigere 'to correct'.
common_mistakes: Confusing corrective with correctional, which refers to prisons and jails.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying KOR-ek-tiv instead of kuh-REK-tiv.

senses.definition: To give off light; to reflect in flashes; to sparkle.
To exhibit brilliant technique or style.
senses.example: The young pianist began to coruscate through the difficult passages, dazzling the audience with every run.

core.definition: To flash or sparkle with bright, quick flashes of light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, KAR-. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable rhymes with 'mate.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests beauty, brilliance, or dazzling skill, usually in descriptive or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use coruscate in speech; it appears in literary criticism, essays, and poetry, often for stars, jewels, or a brilliant speaker. A plain American speaker would say 'sparkle' or 'glitter' instead. Using it in casual talk can sound showy, so keep it for writing or formal praise.

distinctions.note: Sparkle is everyday and general; coruscate is literary and suggests more intense, brilliant flashes.
Glitter often implies showy surface shine; coruscate emphasizes repeated flashes of light, and sometimes of wit or skill.
Glimmer means faint, steady light; coruscate describes brighter, more dazzling flashes.

examples.professional: The keynote speaker's slides didn't coruscate, but her data story was clear and memorable.
examples.analytical: In his essays, the critic lets each paragraph coruscate with unexpected images that reward close reading.

nuance.analogy: To coruscate is like a diamond turned in sunlight: it throws off quick, bright flashes from many facets.
nuance.etymology: From Latin coruscare, 'to vibrate, glitter, flash.'
common_mistakes: Using coruscate in casual speech where sparkle is more natural.
Confusing coruscate with corrugate, a different verb meaning to form ridges.
Putting the stress on the second syllable, as kuh-RUS-kayt.

coruscate.etymology: From Latin *coruscātus*, perfect passive participle of *coruscō* (“to flash, gleam”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: In a right triangle, the ratio of the length of the side adjacent to an acute angle to the length of the hypotenuse. Symbol: cos.

core.definition: In a right triangle, the ratio of the length of the side next to an acute angle to the length of the hypotenuse. Symbol: cos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the first vowel as a long oh. The final 'sine' rhymes with 'line' and should not be pronounced with a separate 'e'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cosine in high school trigonometry, engineering, physics and data science. In speech people often say 'cos' or 'the cosine of theta' in formulas. The word is always neutral and technical, so no social register issues arise.

distinctions.note: Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, while cosine uses the adjacent side, so they are complementary in a right triangle.
Tangent is the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side, so it does not use the hypotenuse at all.

examples.everyday: My son's homework asked for the cosine of a forty-five degree angle, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: We used cosine similarity to compare the embedding vectors, so documents with similar wording scored close to one.
examples.analytical: The law of cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem by adding a term that depends on the cosine of the included angle.

nuance.analogy: If the hypotenuse is a ladder leaning against a wall, the cosine tells you how far the foot of the ladder is from the wall, relative to the ladder's full length.
nuance.etymology: From Latin complementi sinus, meaning the sine of the complement, because cosine of an angle equals sine of its complement.
common_mistakes: Confusing cosine with sine, since both are ratios with the hypotenuse but use different sides.
Pronouncing the word with the stress on the second syllable.
patterns: cosine similarity between A and B

cosine.etymology: From *co* + *sine*, short for *complementi sinus* in Latin, meaning “sine of the complement”.

senses.definition: The study of the physical universe, its structure, dynamics, origin and evolution, and fate.
A metaphysical study into the origin and nature of the universe.
A particular view (cultural or religious) of the structure and origin of the universe.
senses.example: Her sermon contrasted the medieval cosmology of concentric spheres with modern physics.

core.definition: The scientific and philosophical study of the universe's origin, structure, evolution and eventual fate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'MAH', and the final syllable is 'jee'. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'luh-juh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American universities, cosmology is a branch of astronomy and physics, and cosmologists study the Big Bang and dark energy. The word can also refer to a culture's view of the universe, as in 'Mayan cosmology'. Use it neutrally in academic and everyday talk about science.

distinctions.note: Astronomy studies celestial objects such as stars and planets, while cosmology studies the universe as a whole, including its origin and large-scale structure.
Cosmogony is specifically about the origin of the universe, while cosmology covers its structure, evolution and fate as well.

examples.everyday: My brother got really into cosmology after watching documentaries about black holes and the Big Bang.
examples.professional: Our research group uses large simulation datasets to test models in observational cosmology.
examples.analytical: A theological cosmology must explain how creation depends on God while still making sense of the scientific account of the universe's history.

nuance.analogy: If astronomy is a field guide to individual birds, cosmology is the study of the entire ecosystem and how it began and changes over time.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kosmos, meaning order or world, plus logia, meaning study.
common_mistakes: Confusing cosmology with cosmetology, the study of beauty treatments.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'KAHZ-muh-lah-jee'.

cosmology.etymology: From Medieval Latin *cosmologia*, from Ancient Greek *κόσμος* (“world”) + *-λογία* (“treating of”), combination form of *-λόγος* (“one who speaks”).

senses.definition: Assistance (especially from a professional) in the resolution of personal difficulties.

core.definition: Professional help from a trained counselor that supports people in resolving personal, emotional, or family difficulties.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOWN. The American spelling has one l, and the final syllable is a short ling, not long lee. Avoid saying kown-sell-ing with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests support and help, though some people still feel stigma about it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm going to counseling or I'm in counseling to mean regular sessions with a therapist or counselor, often at a school, church, clinic, or workplace. It is less clinical than psychotherapy. Common forms include marriage counseling, grief counseling, and career counseling. If someone mentions it, a natural response is Good for you, or How's it going?

distinctions.note: Therapy is the broader clinical treatment, often by licensed therapists; counseling is often shorter-term and focused on specific problems.
Coaching focuses on goals and performance, while counseling deals more with emotions and personal difficulties.
Advice is one-time guidance from anyone, while counseling is structured professional support over a series of sessions.

examples.everyday: She started counseling after her divorce, and she says it has helped more than she expected.
examples.professional: Our employee assistance program offers free counseling sessions, so contact HR if you would like to book one.
examples.analytical: Pastoral counseling draws on theology and psychology, but its success depends on the counselee's willingness to engage honestly.

nuance.analogy: Counseling is like physical therapy for the mind: a guided practice that builds strength over time.
nuance.etymology: From counsel, from Latin consilium, with the suffix -ing forming a noun for an activity.
common_mistakes: Spelling it counseling with two l's in American writing; the American spelling is counseling.
Using counseling for a single piece of advice; the word refers to an ongoing professional service.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being covert.

core.definition: The quality of being hidden or secret, so that something is not easily seen or known.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KOH. The -tness ending is often pronounced quickly, with the t barely heard and the ending sounding like 'tnuss.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it usually carries a hint of suspicion or secrecy, especially in discussions of intelligence or policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use covertness in everyday speech; they say secrecy or the fact that something was secret. It appears in reports, analysis, and academic writing about how something was hidden, and it is more common in discussions of military, intelligence, or research practices. In a casual conversation, say the secrecy instead.

distinctions.note: Secrecy is the everyday, general word for keeping things hidden, while covertness is more technical and stresses the quality of being hidden from view.
Concealment refers to the act of hiding something, while covertness describes the quality or condition of being hidden.
Discretion means careful, tactful behavior about private matters, and it is usually positive, while covertness is neutral or negative.

examples.professional: The covertness of the data collection raised ethical questions that our review board needed to resolve.
examples.analytical: The covertness of the operation, not its legality, is what makes the author's argument about institutional trust so troubling.

nuance.analogy: Covertness is like a dark room in a house: it is part of the building, but you cannot see into it from the hallway.
nuance.etymology: From covert (adjective) plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using covertness for a single act of hiding; the noun names the quality, not the act.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
Using covertness in casual talk where secrecy sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The state of being creamy.

core.definition: The quality of being smooth, rich and soft in texture, like cream.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KREE. The second syllable is a short, reduced ih, and the final syllable is a weak nus, not 'ness' with a strong e.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is used to praise the texture of food, drink or sauces.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use creaminess mainly for food and drink, as in 'the creaminess of the soup' or 'a dish with great creaminess.' It is a compliment in restaurant reviews and cooking shows. It is rarely used for people or abstract things.

distinctions.note: Smoothness describes the absence of lumps or roughness; creaminess adds the sense of richness and fat.

examples.everyday: The mashed potatoes had a wonderful creaminess that made the whole meal.
examples.professional: The test kitchen approved the new sauce once we adjusted the creaminess without adding more fat.
examples.analytical: The critic measured the dish's success by its balance of acidity and creaminess, which she considered central to its texture.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-made custard that coats the spoon with smooth richness.
nuance.etymology: Formed from cream with the adjective suffix -y and the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full ee, which makes it sound like 'KREE-mee-nes'.
Using creaminess to describe a person's personality; use warmth or kindness instead.

senses.definition: A descendant of European settlers who is born in a colonized country.
senses.example: Her ancestors were Creole planters whose families had lived in Saint-Domingue for generations.

senses.definition: Anyone with mixed ancestry born in a country colonized by Europeans, now especially one who speaks a creole language.
senses.example: My friend, a Creole from Cape Verde, switches between Portuguese and Kriolu at family dinners.

senses.definition: Someone of African descent who is born in the Caribbean or Americas (originally as opposed to an African immigrant).
senses.example: In the 1800s, many Creoles of African descent in Haiti owned small businesses in Port-au-Prince.

senses.definition: A native-born of Francophone descent in the Louisiana territory of any race, as opposed to Anglo-American settlers.
senses.example: Her great-grandfather was a Louisiana Creole who farmed sugarcane along the Bayou Teche.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or characteristic of someone who is a Creole.
senses.example: She inherited a Creole family cookbook filled with recipes from her grandmother's kitchen.

senses.definition: That is a Creole; especially, born in a colonized country different from that of his or her ancestors.
senses.example: Born in Martinique to French parents, he considered himself a Creole artist.

senses.definition: Designating a creolized language.
senses.example: The linguist studied the Creole language that developed on the plantations.

senses.definition: Prepared according to a cooking style developed in a Creole area, now especially that of Louisiana, characterized by a mixture of European and African influences.
senses.example: The restaurant serves shrimp Creole with rice and a rich tomato sauce.

core.definition: A person of mixed European and African descent from Louisiana or the Caribbean, or a language formed by mixing two languages.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, KREE, and the final syllable is 'ohl', with a clear 'oh' vowel and a dark l. Do not say 'kree-OLE' with stress on the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive as a cultural or culinary identity, but sensitive when used as an ethnic label.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, Creole is most common in Louisiana, especially New Orleans, where it refers to a people, a culture, a cuisine and a language. Creole cooking, such as shrimp Creole or gumbo, is a common everyday menu term. As an identity label, people usually use it about themselves, so be careful when you use it about others.

distinctions.note: Cajun refers to the descendants of Acadian settlers in rural Louisiana, while Creole refers to people of mixed European and African descent in New Orleans and the Caribbean; the two cuisines overlap but are different.
A pidgin is a simplified language with no native speakers, while a creole is a fully developed language with native speakers.

examples.everyday: We ordered gumbo and shrimp Creole at a little place near the French Quarter.
examples.professional: Our client's cookbook on Creole cooking is being translated into French for the Louisiana market.
examples.analytical: Linguists distinguish a creole, which developed from contact between groups and has native speakers, from a pidgin, which lacks native speakers.

nuance.analogy: Like a new recipe that blends two family traditions into something that is neither one nor the other.
nuance.etymology: From French créole, from Spanish criollo, a person born in the colonies, ultimately from Portuguese crioulo.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'kree-OHL'.
Using Creole as a general term for any mixed-race person outside Louisiana or the Caribbean.

senses.definition: Sad because of a disappointment.

core.definition: Sad and disappointed, especially after failing at something or hearing bad news.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KREST. The second syllable 'fall' has the aw vowel, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa followed by n.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes sadness and loss of confidence after disappointment, often with a sympathetic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crestfallen' to describe someone who looks visibly disappointed, such as a child who lost a game or a candidate who did not win. It is more common in writing and storytelling than in casual talk, where people often say 'bummed' or 'really disappointed.' It sounds slightly expressive and warm, not harsh.

distinctions.note: Sad is a general word for unhappiness, while crestfallen specifically describes disappointment that shows in one's posture or face.
Disappointed is the everyday, neutral term, while crestfallen is more vivid and suggests visible dejection.

examples.everyday: He looked crestfallen when he got home, because he had not made the team.
examples.professional: After the client rejected our proposal, the crestfallen team spent the afternoon reviewing what went wrong.
examples.analytical: The character's crestfallen silence reveals a deeper disappointment in his own ideals rather than only in the outcome.

nuance.analogy: Crestfallen is like a rooster whose comb has drooped: the pride that stood up straight has collapsed.
nuance.etymology: From crest, the top of a bird's head, and fallen, from the image of a drooping comb after defeat.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'crest-fallen' with a hyphen in careful writing; the standard spelling is one word, 'crestfallen.'
Using it for anger; it describes disappointment and sadness, not frustration.

crestfallen.etymology: From *crest* + *fallen*, from the appearance of a horse with its crest on its chest after defeat in a battle.

senses.definition: To pass from one side or area, physical or abstract, to another.
senses.example: To reach the other bank of the river, we tried crossing over on a log.

senses.definition: To die.
senses.example: Sarah's grandmother crossed over last night.

core.definition: To move from one side, place, or group to another. Also, euphemistically, to die.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OH in over, and the final r is clearly pronounced in American English. Keep cross lighter and avoid saying 'OH-vair' or 'krawss-OH-ver' with equal stress on both words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. The sense of dying is a gentle euphemism and is best kept for religious or sympathetic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cross over for physically going from one side to another, such as a street, a bridge, or a border, and for changing category, like moving from one job field to another. The phrase 'he crossed over' for death is common in church and family conversation but would sound odd in a business meeting. The phrasal verb is intransitive, so you usually say 'cross over to the other side' rather than 'cross over the street'.

distinctions.note: Go across is the most neutral description of moving over a space. Cross over often suggests a clearer boundary or a change of side or category.
Cross can be used with an object, as in 'cross the street,' while cross over is usually followed by to, into, or nothing at all.

collocations: cross over to the other side
cross over into a new market
cross over from academia to industry

examples.everyday: Wait for the walk signal, then cross over to the other side of Main Street.
examples.professional: Once the pilot team is comfortable, we will cross over from the old reporting system to the new one next quarter.
examples.analytical: Such arguments often cross over from empirical claims into moral conclusions without any justification being offered.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge: you start on one bank and end up on the other.
nuance.etymology: Cross comes from Old English cros, from Old Norse kross, probably from Latin crux; over is from Old English ofer.
common_mistakes: Using a preposition after the verb with an object, as in 'cross over the street'; say 'cross the street' or 'cross over to the other side'.
Stressing cross equally with over, which makes the phrase sound unnatural.

synonyms: go to be with the Lord
cross-over.etymology: * From the belief that the soul of the dead crosses over a river when one dies.

senses.definition: Across or between more than one mode.
senses.example: The cross-modal study showed that listeners recognized voices more accurately when they could also see the speaker's face.

core.definition: Relating or linking different types of input or senses, such as text and images in AI, or sight and sound in perception.

pronunciation.tip: The strong stress falls on MOH in 'modal', and 'cross' takes a lighter secondary stress. Keep the 'r' in 'cross' audible, and make the second syllable a simple 'dul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cross-modal' mainly in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence, especially in phrases like 'cross-modal retrieval' for matching text and images. In AI papers, 'multimodal' is also common, but 'cross-modal' emphasizes transfer or matching between modalities. Use it in technical writing and talks rather than casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Multimodal describes systems that use several input types together, while cross-modal stresses relationships or transfers between modalities.
Intermodal refers to moving goods between transport modes like truck and rail, which is a different domain entirely.

examples.everyday: My kid swears the song tastes like grape, which is kind of a cross-modal thing going on in her head.
examples.professional: The model supports cross-modal retrieval, so a text query can return the most relevant images from the catalog.
examples.analytical: Cross-modal correspondences in perception suggest that the brain links shape and sound before conscious reflection.

nuance.analogy: Like a translator who turns meaning from one language into another, but between senses or data types.
nuance.etymology: Cross from Old English cros, borrowed from Old Norse kross; modal from Latin modus, 'measure or manner'.
common_mistakes: Using 'cross-modal' for multiple inputs at once; for that, say 'multimodal'.
Stressing 'cross' too heavily, so the word sounds like 'KRAWS-MOH-dul'.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of cubitus.

core.definition: The chemical symbol for copper, the reddish metal used in wiring, plumbing and many alloys.

pronunciation.tip: Read the two letters C and U as their letter names, with the main stress on the second letter, YOO. Americans don't say copper when reading the symbol aloud in a chemistry class.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific symbol with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Cu in chemistry, physics and materials science, such as on the periodic table and in formulas. In everyday speech, people say copper. The sense 'cubitus', an anatomical abbreviation, is rare and not used in ordinary American English, so it is omitted here. Write it with a capital C and lowercase u, since the case matters.

distinctions.note: C is the symbol for carbon, a different element, so the second letter u tells you the element is copper.

examples.everyday: My chemistry homework asks what Cu stands for, and it's copper, the reddish metal in old pennies.
examples.professional: Our catalyst is copper-doped zinc oxide, so we track the Cu loading in every batch before testing.
examples.analytical: The Cu(II) complex shows a characteristic d-d absorption band, which reflects the electronic configuration of the copper ion.

nuance.analogy: Like a short nickname for copper on the periodic table, a label that stands for the whole element.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cuprum, copper, from Cyprium aes, metal of Cyprus.
common_mistakes: Writing CU, which in texts or business means see you or credit union; Cu is the chemical symbol.
Pronouncing it as coo or as copper when reading the symbol aloud in a science setting.

senses.definition: A blind alley or dead end street.
A circular area at the end of a dead end street to allow cars to turn around, designed so children can play on the street, with little or no through-traffic.
An impasse.
senses.example: Our negotiations hit a cul-de-sac when neither side would move on the budget.

senses.definition: A sacklike cavity, a tube open at one end only.
senses.example: The surgeon explained that the abscess formed a small cul-de-sac beneath the gum line.

core.definition: A dead-end street that is closed at one end, usually with a circular area at the end where cars can turn around.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Americans say the final part as 'sak', rhyming with 'back', not the French 'sahk'. The middle 'de' is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. In American suburbs, a cul-de-sac suggests quiet, safety, and a friendly neighborhood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cul-de-sac' every day when giving directions or describing a neighborhood. It is common in home listings and on maps. In some parts of the country, a closed street is simply called a 'dead end' or 'court'. The word also has a figurative sense, 'an impasse', but that is less common.

distinctions.note: A dead end is any street that stops, while a cul-de-sac is a specific type with a turnaround. 'Dead end' is more general and everyday.
A loop curves and comes back to the main road, while a cul-de-sac has only one entrance.

collocations: at the end of the cul-de-sac

examples.everyday: We moved to a cul-de-sac so the kids can ride their bikes without much traffic.
examples.professional: The city planner approved a new cul-de-sac for the subdivision to give emergency vehicles room to turn around.
examples.analytical: The cul-de-sac became a symbol of suburban planning, trading through-traffic for privacy and a sense of community.

nuance.analogy: A cul-de-sac is like the bottom of a bag: the road goes in and has to turn around.
nuance.etymology: From French, literally 'bottom of a bag', from cul 'bottom' and sac 'bag'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a French 'sahk' ending instead of 'sak'.
Using it for any dead-end street, when Americans would usually say 'dead end' in general.
Dropping the hyphens in writing, though spacing is common in informal writing.

senses.definition: Providing protection, care, supervision or guarding.
senses.example: custodial account, custodial care

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to or providing custody, especially of a child.
senses.example: custodial dispute, custodial parent, custodial guardian

senses.definition: Providing punishment by incarceration.
senses.example: custodial sentence, custodial status

senses.definition: Occurring while in custody.
senses.example: custodial interrogation, custodial rape

senses.definition: Related to the work of a custodian.
senses.example: custodial closet, custodial area

core.definition: Relating to the legal care or guardianship of someone, especially a child, or to the supervised care of a person or property.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STOH, and the first syllable is a weak kuh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in legal and social contexts it describes responsibility rather than judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use custodial most often in custodial parent, custodial care and custodial staff. A custodial parent is the one who has the child day to day, a term used constantly in family court. Custodial staff means janitorial or cleaning workers in schools and offices, so the phrase does not mean prison guards in everyday US speech.

distinctions.note: Custodial is the adjective, used for things like custodial care or custodial duties; custodian is the person who holds the role.
Custodial refers to day-to-day physical care; guardianship is the broader legal authority to make decisions for someone who cannot.

examples.everyday: Since she's the custodial parent, the kids live with her during the school week.
examples.professional: Our custodial staff handles the building's cleaning and the weekend maintenance checks.
examples.analytical: The institution's custodial logic treats protection as a duty owed to those in its care, not a favor it chooses to grant.

nuance.analogy: A custodial relationship is like a house-sitter's job: you are responsible for the house, but you do not own it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin custodia, 'guarding', from custos, 'guard', with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using custodial as a noun; the person is a custodian, and custodial only describes things like care or duties.
Assuming custodial staff means prison guards; in US schools and offices it means janitorial workers.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to the complex roots of unity.
Of, or relating to cyclotomy.

core.definition: Relating to the complex roots of unity, or to the division of a circle into equal parts in number theory.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TAH, the third syllable. Americans pronounce the 'o' in the middle of 'cyclo' as a long 'oh', and the final syllable is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Only mathematicians and advanced students use this word, typically in number theory and algebra. Americans would rarely use it in conversation, and a general audience would not understand it without explanation. In a graduate seminar or a paper, it is the correct term.

distinctions.note: Cyclic means repeating or circular in general, while cyclotomic is a precise term about roots of unity and dividing a circle.
Circular refers to a round shape in everyday speech, while cyclotomic is a technical term from algebra and geometry.

examples.everyday: My son's math homework used the word cyclotomic, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: Our cryptography team studied cyclotomic fields because they simplify certain modular calculations.
examples.analytical: The cyclotomic polynomial of order n has as its roots exactly the primitive nth roots of unity.

nuance.analogy: A cyclotomic polynomial is like a set of evenly spaced markers around a clock face, each one a distinct point on the circle.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kyklos, 'circle', and tomē, 'cutting', via cyclotomy, the division of a circle.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'sy-kloh-TOH-mik'; the stress belongs on the 'tah' syllable.
Using it as a general synonym for 'cyclic' or 'circular' in ordinary speech.

senses.definition: To make slightly wet or soiled by spattering or sprinkling a liquid (such as water, mud, or paint) on it; to bedabble.
senses.example: The careless painter dabbled his sleeves with blue paint while cleaning the brushes.

senses.definition: To cause splashing by moving a body part like a bill or limb in soft mud, water, etc. often playfully; to play in shallow water; to paddle.
senses.example: The children sat on the dock and dabbled their feet in the water.

senses.definition: To feed without diving, by submerging the head and neck underwater to seek food, often also tipping up the tail straight upwards above the water.
senses.example: Along the pond, the ducks dabble for pondweed while their tails point straight up.

senses.definition: To participate or have an interest in an activity in a casual or superficial way.
senses.example: She’s an actress by trade, but has been known to dabble in poetry.

senses.definition: A spattering or sprinkling of a liquid.
senses.example: A dabble of mud on her white sneakers showed she had crossed the creek.

senses.definition: An act of splashing in soft mud, water, etc.
senses.example: The kids enjoyed a happy dabble in the shallow water near the dock.

senses.definition: An act of participation in an activity in a casual or superficial way.
senses.example: He enjoyed a dabble in politics before deciding that consulting was more his speed.

core.definition: To take part in an activity casually or without serious commitment, or to splash lightly in water or mud.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'l' with a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'DAB-uhl.' Do not add an extra vowel between 'b' and 'l.'

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or neutral; it suggests a casual, shallow involvement rather than serious work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dabble to describe trying an interest or skill without going deep, such as dabbling in painting or cooking. It sounds friendly and modest, and it can be a polite way to say you are not an expert. People might say they 'dabble in the stock market' to signal small, casual investments. Avoid using it for serious professional work, where it can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: Tinker suggests making small adjustments to improve something, while dabble suggests trying something out without depth.

examples.everyday: I dabble in gardening on weekends, but I still buy most of my vegetables at the farmers market.
examples.professional: Our team dabbles in machine learning, but the core product still relies on traditional statistical models.
examples.analytical: Philosophers who only dabble in ethics often miss the deep tensions that specialists have spent decades analyzing.

nuance.analogy: To dabble is like dipping one toe into a lake before deciding whether to swim.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English dabelen, a frequentative of dabben, to splash.
common_mistakes: Using 'dabble on' instead of 'dabble in' with an activity.
Pronouncing it 'DAB-ble' with a clearly pronounced extra vowel.

senses.definition: A descendant of Dan, fifth son of Jacob.
A descendant or member of the tribe of Dan.
(historical) A member of a fraternal vigilante group founded by members of the Latter Day Saints in the 1830s.
senses.example: Historians say a Danite band in Missouri used threats and violence against dissenters.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to Dan, or to the tribe of Dan.
senses.example: Scholars traced the Danite migration northward during the late Bronze Age.

core.definition: A member of the tribe of Dan, one of the twelve tribes of ancient Israel descended from Jacob's son Dan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable rhymes with 'bite'. Do not add an extra syllable like 'dan-EYE-tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in biblical and historical use, though the 19th-century Latter-day Saint group is controversial.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Danite' mainly in biblical studies and in discussions of Latter-day Saint history. In a Bible study, it simply names a tribe. When discussing the 1830s group, add context, since the term has a violent history. Most people would say 'a member of the tribe of Dan' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Dan is the son of Jacob or the tribe's name; Danite is the term for a member or descendant of that tribe.
Danish relates to Denmark, a common confusion with no connection to the tribe.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we talked about the Danites, who had a hard time finding land of their own.
examples.professional: In the seminar I'll cover the Danites, tracing the tribe's shifting settlements in the book of Judges.
examples.analytical: The Danite migration in Judges 18 serves as a narrative of violent expansion that the text presents without clear approval.

nuance.analogy: A Danite is like a member of a family line named after an ancestor, carrying the name of a founder across generations.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Dan, meaning judge or he has judged, plus the English suffix -ite, meaning a member of.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'Danish', which refers to Denmark.
Saying 'DAN-eye-ite' with an extra syllable instead of the two-syllable 'DAN-ight'.
nuance.biblical_note: Dan was the fifth son of Jacob, born to Bilhah, Rachel's servant. The Hebrew name Dan means judge, and the tribe's name is connected to the verb din, to judge. Key passages include Genesis 30:6, where Dan's birth is explained as God judging Rachel's case; Genesis 49:16-18, Jacob's blessing where Dan will judge his people; and Judges 18, where the Danites seek new land, seize the city of Laish, and set up an idol.

senses.definition: A source of data; typically a database.

core.definition: Any origin from which data is obtained, such as a database, file, sensor or API.

pronunciation.tip: 'Source' is one syllable in American speech, SAWRS, with a rhotic r and the vowel of 'caught'. Don't add a vowel after the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a technical origin without judgment, though a questionable source can prompt doubts about the findings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'data source' in IT, research, business and journalism, and in analytics tools people 'connect to a data source'. In practice the term covers far more than databases, including spreadsheets, sensors and web APIs. In everyday talk, people ask 'Where's the data source for that claim?' and a natural answer is 'It's the state's annual report.'

distinctions.note: A data set is the data itself, while a data source is the place it comes from.
A database is one kind of data source; sources can also include files, sensors and web services.

examples.everyday: Before you trust that headline, check the data source, because the poll was paid for by the company selling the product.
examples.professional: We need to connect the dashboard to a verified data source instead of the exported spreadsheet.
examples.analytical: The validity of any argument rests on its data source, since a biased origin can make a sound method produce false conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Like the spring that feeds a river: what flows downstream depends entirely on what comes out of it at the start.
nuance.etymology: Source comes from Old French sorse, 'a rising, a spring', from Latin surgere, 'to rise'.
common_mistakes: Using 'data source' to mean the data itself; the data set is the data, and the source is where it comes from.
Adding a vowel and saying SOR-suss; in American speech the word is one syllable, SAWRS.

senses.definition: A non-clerical role for women in some churches.
senses.example: She served as a deaconess at her church, visiting members who were homebound.

senses.definition: (rare) A female deacon.
senses.example: The bishop ordained her as a deaconess, the first woman in the diocese to serve.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A female servant in the early Christian church.
senses.example: Phoebe is described in Romans as a deaconess serving the church at Cenchreae.

senses.definition: The nun in charge of the altar in a convent.
senses.example: The deaconess carefully arranged the linens and candles on the convent altar each morning.

senses.definition: One of an order of women in some Protestant churches who nurse the sick and tend the poor.
senses.example: The deaconess visited the sick ward every afternoon, bringing soup and prayers to the poor.

core.definition: A woman who serves in a church in a ministry of service and charity, sometimes formally commissioned or ordained, depending on the denomination.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the last syllable, 'NESS,' with a secondary stress on 'dee.' Do not put the stress on 'dee' as in 'deacon.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; evokes service, though some find the term dated where women serve as deacons.
nuance.usage_note: Some churches, such as Lutheran and Methodist ones, have formal deaconess orders. Many churches now simply say 'deacon' for both men and women. Choose the term the particular church uses.

distinctions.note: Deacon is the general office; deaconess specifically marks a woman and may denote a distinct, non-clergy role.
A nun belongs to a religious order under vows, while a deaconess serves in the church without necessarily taking monastic vows.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a deaconess and visited sick members every week.
examples.professional: The seminary offers a program that prepares students for ministry as pastors or deaconesses.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether Phoebe in Romans 16 held a formal office or served informally as a deaconess.

nuance.etymology: From deacon plus the feminine suffix -ess, from Late Latin diaconissa.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'DEE-kuh-ness'; stress the last syllable.
Assuming it always means an ordained clergy member; it often does not.
nuance.biblical_note: Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae; the RSV renders it 'deaconess,' while the Greek word is the same as for male deacons. 1 Timothy 3:11 mentions 'women' (or deacons' wives) in the context of deacon qualifications, and translators differ on its meaning.

traditions.view: The early church had ordained deaconesses who assisted with women's baptism and care; the order is not widely active today, though some call for its revival.
Women deacons existed in the early church, but today the diaconate is limited to men. The question of women deacons has been studied by commissions.
Practice differs: Lutheran deaconess communities exist, Methodist and Anglican churches may ordain or consecrate women as deacons, and many Baptist churches have women deacons or none.

senses.definition: To participate in a debate; to dispute, argue, especially in a public arena.
senses.example: "Debate me, coward!" snarled the completely normal intellectual.

senses.definition: To consider (to oneself), to think over, to attempt to decide.
senses.example: He was debating where he'd spend his holiday.

senses.definition: An argument, or discussion, usually in an ordered or formal setting, often with more than two people, generally ending with a vote or other decision.
senses.example: After a four-hour debate, the committee voted to table the motion.

senses.definition: An informal and spirited but generally civil discussion of opposing views.
senses.example: The debate over the age of the universe is thousands of years old.

senses.definition: Discussion of opposing views.
senses.example: There has been considerable debate concerning exactly how to format these articles.

senses.definition: A type of literary composition, taking the form of a discussion or disputation, commonly found in the vernacular medieval poetry of many European countries, as well as in medieval Latin.
senses.example: Medieval poets wrote many debates between the owl and the nightingale.

core.definition: To discuss opposing views in a structured way; also, a formal or heated discussion of opposing positions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -BAYT. The first syllable is a weak, reduced vowel, so do not stress DE- as in some other English words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when it means a healthy exchange of ideas and negative when it means endless bickering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'debate about', 'debate over', or 'debate whether' with a clause, and 'debate with someone' for a face-to-face argument. The idiom 'that's up for debate' means that something is not settled. A natural reply is 'Fair point, let's talk about it.'

distinctions.note: Argue is more general and can be personal or angry, while debate implies a structured or public discussion of opposing sides.
Discuss is more neutral and less adversarial, while debate suggests opposing positions and a contest of reasons.
Dispute is more formal and often about facts, claims, or legal rights, while debate is usually about ideas or options.

examples.everyday: We debated where to eat for an hour, and then we just got pizza.
examples.professional: The product team is debating whether to ship the feature in June or wait for the security review.
examples.analytical: Philosophers continue to debate whether moral facts exist independently of human minds.

nuance.analogy: A debate is like a tennis match of ideas: each side sends its arguments back and forth until someone scores a point or the referee calls it.
nuance.etymology: Debate comes from Old French debatre, to fight or beat down, from de- and batre, to beat.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I debated about going' when 'I debated whether to go' is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable as in DE-bate, which is a common mistake among learners.

debate.etymology: From Middle English *debaten*, from Old French *debatre* (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic, from Latin *dis-* (“apart, in different directions”) + *battuō* (“to beat, to fence”).

senses.definition: The act or process of decelerating.
senses.example: The rocket is now in deceleration.

senses.definition: The amount by which a speed or velocity decreases (and so a scalar quantity or a vector quantity), an acceleration having a negative numerical value.
senses.example: The brakes produce a deceleration of 10 meters per second.

core.definition: The process of slowing down, or the amount by which speed decreases over time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RAY, the fourth syllable. The earlier syllables are lighter, and the 'r' is clear in American speech, so do not let it disappear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is precise and objective, and it is used in physics, engineering, and economics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deceleration mainly in physics, engineering, cars, sports science, and economics, as in 'deceleration in job growth.' In everyday talk, people usually say 'slowing down,' 'braking,' or 'losing speed.' Using deceleration in casual conversation may sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: Braking is the act of using the brakes, while deceleration is any decrease in speed, whatever the cause.
Slowdown is informal and general, often used for traffic or the economy, while deceleration is more technical and precise.

examples.everyday: The car felt a sudden deceleration when the driver hit the brakes hard.
examples.professional: The model flagged a sharp deceleration in user growth over the last two quarters.
examples.analytical: Physicists define deceleration as acceleration opposite to the direction of motion, so a negative value means the speed is shrinking.

nuance.analogy: Like a brake pedal that gradually pulls back the speed instead of cutting it off.
nuance.etymology: From Latin de- 'down' plus celerare 'to hasten,' from celer 'swift.'
common_mistakes: Using deceleration in casual conversation where 'slowing down' sounds more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'dih-SEL-uh-ray-shun.'

senses.definition: A person or object meant to lure somebody into danger.
A real or fake animal used by hunters to lure game.
senses.example: The hunter placed a wooden decoy of a mallard near the pond to lure ducks in.

senses.definition: Deceptive military device used to draw enemy attention or fire away from a more important target.
senses.example: The fighter jets released radar decoys to draw the enemy missiles away from the bombers.

senses.definition: An assembly of hooped or netted corridors into which wild ducks may be enticed (originally by tame ducks) and trapped.
senses.example: Our local historical society restored an old decoy where ducks were once trapped in netted hoops.

senses.definition: To lead into danger by artifice; to lure into a net or snare; to entrap.
senses.example: to decoy troops into an ambush; to decoy ducks into a net

senses.definition: To act as, or use, a decoy.
senses.example: As they were being decoyed, the rescue team carried the hostage and quietly slipped away.

core.definition: A person or object used to trick or lure someone or something into a trap, danger, or wrong position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable in the noun. As a verb, Americans stress the second syllable: 'dih-KOY'. The item's schwa-initial form is the verb pattern, so use the stress shift for the noun.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it implies deception, though a decoy may be used for protection or sport.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'decoy' for hunting decoys, police or military tactics, and figurative talk about a distraction. Phrases like 'decoy car' or 'be a decoy' are common in news and movies. In casual talk, saying someone 'was used as a decoy' implies they were deliberately used to draw attention.

distinctions.note: 'Bait' is food or a lure used to catch something; 'decoy' is a fake or misleading object or person that imitates a target.
A 'distraction' simply diverts attention, while a 'decoy' is deliberately designed to lure into danger or away from a target.

examples.everyday: The hunter set up a wooden duck decoy near the pond to attract the birds.
examples.professional: Our security team used a decoy account to see whether the phishing emails would reach the real staff.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the tempting promise as a decoy, leading the reader away from the deeper question of what makes life meaningful.

nuance.analogy: A decoy is like a fake cake left on a table to tempt a thief away from the real treasure.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch de kooi, 'the decoy cage', from Latin cavea, 'cage'.
common_mistakes: Using the verb pronunciation for the noun; the noun stresses the first syllable.
Confusing 'decoy' with 'bait', which is used to catch something directly.

senses.definition: In a defensible manner.
Defendably.

core.definition: In a way that can be justified or reasonably defended.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the stem, FEN. The final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a choice or claim is reasonable, though not necessarily perfect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use defensibly in formal writing, reviews, and analysis to say something can be reasonably justified. It is rare in casual speech; in conversation people usually say 'reasonably' or 'you can make a case for it'. Avoid the nonstandard 'defendably' in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Reasonably is the everyday choice; defensibly is more formal and implies the position would survive criticism.
Justifiably stresses that good grounds exist; defensibly stresses that the position can be held against objections.

examples.professional: We can defensibly exclude those outliers, since they come from a broken sensor.
examples.analytical: The author defensibly argues that moral intuitions carry evidential weight, even if they cannot be fully systematized.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence built on solid posts: it stands up to a push because the structure is sound.
nuance.etymology: From defensible, from defend, from Latin defendere, plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'defendably', which is nonstandard in formal American English.
Using it in casual speech where 'reasonably' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Great respect.
senses.example: The children treated their elders with deference.

senses.definition: The willingness to carry out the wishes of others.
senses.example: By tidying his room, he showed deference to his mother.

core.definition: Polite respect for someone's wishes, authority, or expertise, often shown by yielding to them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DEF. The middle syllable is reduced to 'er', and the final -ence is 'uns'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it shows respect, but it can sound negative if it implies excessive submission.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deference in discussions of hierarchy, expertise, and manners: 'out of deference to her seniority'. In casual speech they often say 'respect' instead. 'Deference' suggests the respect involves yielding to someone's judgment, so it can sound stiff in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Respect is broader and everyday; deference specifically means yielding to another's wishes or authority.
Obedience means following orders; deference is a voluntary yielding out of respect and does not always involve following commands.

examples.everyday: Out of deference to my grandmother, we waited until she sat down before we started eating.
examples.professional: Out of deference to the senior engineers, I held my proposal until they had reviewed the architecture.
examples.analytical: Weber distinguishes legitimate authority from mere habits of deference, asking why people accept rule at all.

nuance.analogy: Like stepping aside at a doorway to let someone pass: the gesture acknowledges their claim to go first.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin deferentia, from Latin deferre 'to bring down, submit, yield'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'DEE-fer-ence'; the stress is on the first syllable, DEF.
Using 'deference' for 'difference' or 'defiance' by mistake; check the spelling.

senses.definition: Empty of all the air or gas that was or could be inside.
senses.example: The tire went flat overnight, and the bike was completely deflated by morning.

senses.definition: Disappointed; depressed, especially after having been hopeful or in high spirits.
senses.example: She felt deflated after the job interview, though she had expected to get the offer.

senses.definition: Reduced or lowered.
senses.example: Attendance at the summer festival was deflated compared with last year's crowd.

senses.definition: Adjusted downward to compensate for inflation.
senses.example: Using the deflated series, real wages grew more slowly than the nominal figures suggested.

senses.definition: Suffering from deflation.
senses.example: Japan's economy remained deflated for years, leaving borrowers squeezed and prices stagnant.

senses.definition: Subsided or compressed downward.
senses.example: The old cake was deflated in the middle where the oven door had slammed.

core.definition: Feeling disappointed, discouraged, or low after hopes were let down; also, having lost its air so that it is flat or soft.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on FLAY, the second syllable, and the ending -ed is pronounced as a short id. Don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a loss of energy or hope, so it sounds sad or discouraging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use deflated for a mood after bad news, such as 'I felt deflated when the game was canceled.' For a ball or tire, casual speakers more often say flat. Don't use it for serious grief; sad, heartbroken, or devastated are better in those cases.

distinctions.note: Disappointed is the general, neutral term, while deflated suggests a sudden loss of energy or confidence after hope.
Flat can mean dull or low in energy, and for a tire it means out of air; deflated is more vivid and emotional when used about feelings.

examples.everyday: I felt pretty deflated when the restaurant was closed after our long drive.
examples.professional: The team looked deflated after the launch slipped to next quarter.
examples.analytical: Her argument leaves the reader deflated, because the promised resolution never arrives.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon left on the floor the day after a party.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of deflate, from Latin de- plus inflare, to blow into.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am deflated' when you mean angry; deflated means disappointed or low, not angry.
Stressing the first syllable: say dih-FLAY-tid, not DEF-lay-tid.

core.definition: A personal name in the Hebrew Bible, borne by several men, including a secretary of King Jehoiakim who opposed the burning of Jeremiah's scroll.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LAY, and end with a light 'uh'. The name has three syllables, not two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name with no everyday sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Delaiah mainly in Bible study, in sermons, or in reference works about biblical names. It is not used in ordinary conversation. Someone might simply say Oh, I remember Delaiah from Jeremiah if the topic comes up.

distinctions.note: The name is shared by several different men in the Bible, so the passage determines which Delaiah is meant.

examples.everyday: Do you remember who Delaiah was in the story of the scroll?
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Delaiah appears as one of the officials who urged the king to spare the scroll.
examples.analytical: The text names Delaiah among the officials who resisted the king's command, which marks him as a moral contrast to the king.

nuance.analogy: Delaiah is like a name on a roll call: it identifies a particular person by reference to a specific moment in the story.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Delayahu, meaning 'Yahweh has drawn out' or 'Yahweh has set free'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as DEL-ay-uh, stressing the first syllable.
Confusing it with Delilah, a different biblical name.
nuance.biblical_note: Delaiah (Hebrew Delayahu, 'Yahweh has drawn out' or 'Yahweh has set free') is the name of several men. In Jeremiah 36:12 and 36:25 Delaiah son of Shemaiah is an official who objects when King Jehoiakim orders Jeremiah's scroll to be burned. In Ezra 2:60 and Nehemiah 7:62, the sons of Delaiah are listed among those who returned from exile in Babylon.

senses.definition: Easily damaged or requiring careful handling.
senses.example: Those clothes are made from delicate lace.

senses.definition: Characterized by a fine structure or thin lines.
senses.example: Her face was delicate.

senses.definition: Intended for use with fragile items.
senses.example: Set the washing machine to the delicate cycle.

senses.definition: Refined; gentle; scrupulous not to trespass or offend; considerate; said of manners, conduct, or feelings.
senses.example: delicate behavior

senses.definition: Of weak health; easily sick; unable to endure hardship.
senses.example: a delicate child
